      "id": "pat-encounter-death-detection",
      "summary": "HP-mutating verbs check post-mutation HP and call private killEntity helper when an entity hits 0; helper publishes EntityDied (per-viewer) → deletes from data → splices Initiative → publishes EntityRemoved (broadcast) → calls checkEncounterEnd",
      "added": "2026-05-09",
      "status": "validated",
      "validated_in": "Wave 2.10 playtest 2026-05-09 (toolkit encounter PR #643)",
      "details": "Shipped in Wave 2.10 (rpg-toolkit PR #643). Death detection lives in the encounter aggregate, gated on HP transitions inside HP-mutating verbs:

  - `TakeAction` — player attacks monster; after applying damage, checks `if monster.HP > 0 → continue, else killEntity(monsterID, playerID as killer)`.
  - `NPCAct` — NPC attacks player; same post-damage check (see partial-coverage reality note pat-encounter-player-death-partial).

The killEntity helper is a single private method that owns the multi-step state mutation:

  func (e *Encounter) killEntity(id core.EntityID, killerID core.EntityID) {
      // 1. Publish EntityDiedEvent — per-viewer (LoS gates whether viewers see the kill itself)
      e.broker.Publish(events.NewEntityDiedEvent(id, killerID, perViewerProjection))

      // 2. Delete from data map (Monsters or Players depending on type)
      delete(e.data.Monsters, id)

      // 3. Splice Initiative — remove id from the slice; adjust ActiveIdx if necessary
      //    (if removed-idx < ActiveIdx, decrement ActiveIdx; if == ActiveIdx, leave it pointing
      //     at the next actor since the dead actor's turn is over)
      e.spliceInitiative(id)

      // 4. Publish EntityRemovedEvent — broadcast (every viewer must drop the entity)
      e.broker.Publish(events.NewEntityRemovedEvent(id))

      // 5. Check encounter-end predicate (see pat-encounter-end-predicate)
      e.checkEncounterEnd()
  }

Why a single private helper: same encapsulation pattern as `OpenDoor` (Wave 2.7). Multi-step state mutation owns its sequence — callers (TakeAction, NPCAct) just say "this entity dies" and the helper handles the four-step ordering. Future verbs that produce kills (cast Fireball, AoE damage, environmental hazards) call killEntity without re-implementing the sequence.

The ordering is load-bearing:
  - EntityDied BEFORE delete: viewers need the entity's last-known data (position, type) to render the death animation; if delete happens first the projection has nothing to attribute to.
  - Delete BEFORE EntityRemoved: the wire event signals "this id is gone" — server state must already match.
  - Splice BEFORE EntityRemoved: clients update initiative display from the broadcast; server-side initiative must be consistent before the event lands.
  - checkEncounterEnd LAST: end-detection reads post-kill state (data.Monsters now-empty if this was the last); must run after delete + splice.

When adding a new kill-source verb in future waves: route through killEntity, not a duplicate sequence. If the new verb needs to suppress the kill (resurrection mid-action, charm-don't-kill), that's a flag on the verb call, not a parallel helper.

Cross-link: api-side pat-v2-cause-effect-death-events (which describes how the two events surface on the wire)."

    {
      "id": "pat-encounter-terminal-mode",
      "summary": "Encounter terminal state is a new mode value (core.ModeEnded); reuses existing mode-gating; verbs return ErrEncounterEnded; mode change clears Initiative + ActiveIdx + Round",
      "added": "2026-05-09",
      "status": "validated",
      "validated_in": "Wave 2.10 playtest 2026-05-09 (toolkit encounter PR #643)",
      "details": "Shipped in Wave 2.10 (rpg-toolkit PR #643). Encounter end is encoded as a third value in the `core.EncounterMode` enum:

  type EncounterMode int
  const (
      ModeUnspecified EncounterMode = iota
      ModeFreeRoam
      ModeTurnBased
      ModeEnded   // Wave 2.10 addition
  )

Design decision (made at PR #643 dispatch — Option A vs separate Status field): chose ModeEnded for parsimony. Existing mode-gating in combat verbs (`if e.Mode() != ModeTurnBased → ErrNotInCombat`) extends naturally — adding `if e.Mode() == ModeEnded → ErrEncounterEnded` at the same gate site is a small additive change. A separate `Status` field would have required new gating everywhere mode is currently checked, doubling the test surface.

Verbs that mutate state (Move, OpenDoor, AttemptUnlock, SubmitCheck, TakeAction, NPCAct, EndTurn, Interact) check terminal state at their entry point:

  if e.data.Mode == core.ModeEnded {
      return ErrEncounterEnded
  }

The rpg-api handler maps ErrEncounterEnded → FailedPrecondition (api pat-v2-terminal-encounter-state).

Mode change to ModeEnded clears volatile turn state:
  - Initiative = nil (no actors in turn order)
  - ActiveIdx = 0 (no active actor)
  - Round = 0 (round counter reset)

The Mode field itself flips and the EncounterEndedEvent fires once (see pat-encounter-end-predicate). Persistence: ToData / LoadFromData round-trip ModeEnded the same way as other mode values.

Wire-projection asymmetry: the v1alpha2 EncounterMode proto enum doesn't yet have an ENCOUNTER_MODE_ENDED value, so the rpg-api translator maps ModeEnded → ENCOUNTER_MODE_FREE_ROAM on the wire. Clients consume the dedicated EncounterEndedEvent for end detection. Reference api pat-v2-mode-ended-wire-mapping. When v1beta proto cuts, ENCOUNTER_MODE_ENDED MAY be added — at which point translator updates to map directly.

Why clear Initiative on end (vs preserve for retry/replay): future replay-after-end use cases (death recap UI, kill-cam) re-render from the event log, not from current state. Clearing keeps current state semantically clean — "no actors are taking turns" is true post-end. Preserving would force every snapshot consumer to disambiguate "actors mid-fight" from "actors who fought and stopped."

When extending: any new turn-state field added in future waves (reaction window, delay/ready actions) should also clear on ModeEnded transition. Keep one rule: end clears all turn-volatile state."

    {
      "id": "pat-encounter-end-predicate",
      "summary": "Encounter-end predicate is len(data.Monsters) == 0 for Wave 2.10; encapsulated in checkEncounterEnd() so future waves swap predicate without touching the kill path; publish-side effects fire only when predicate first goes true",
      "added": "2026-05-09",
      "status": "validated",
      "validated_in": "Wave 2.10 playtest 2026-05-09 (toolkit encounter PR #643)",
      "details": "Shipped in Wave 2.10 (rpg-toolkit PR #643). The encounter-end check is encapsulated in a private method on Encounter:

  func (e *Encounter) checkEncounterEnd() {
      if e.data.Mode == core.ModeEnded {
          return  // already ended; idempotent
      }
      if len(e.data.Monsters) == 0 {
          e.data.Mode = core.ModeEnded
          e.data.Initiative = nil
          e.data.ActiveIdx = 0
          e.data.Round = 0
          e.broker.Publish(events.NewEncounterEndedEvent())  // broadcast, fires ONCE
      }
  }

The predicate (`len(data.Monsters) == 0`) is the Wave 2.10 default — "all monsters dead" ends the encounter. Future waves will swap to other predicates without touching the kill path:

  - Boss-only kill: `data.Monsters[bossID] == nil` (other monsters can flee, only boss kill ends it).
  - Time-out: `data.Round > maxRounds`.
  - Fled-from: `len(data.PlayersInBounds) == 0` for N consecutive rounds.
  - Objective-based: `data.ObjectiveCompleted == true` (capture flag, escape door reached).

Why encapsulated: callers (killEntity in Wave 2.10; future verbs that might end an encounter without a kill — escape-through-door verb, time-advance verb) just call checkEncounterEnd. The predicate logic stays in one place; swap it out for the next wave's design without auditing every kill-path call site.

Predicate evaluation is a PURE FUNCTION (no side effects until the body decides to mutate). The publish-side effects (set ModeEnded, clear turn state, fire EncounterEndedEvent) only happen when the predicate first goes true — the early-return on `data.Mode == ModeEnded` ensures idempotency. Re-calling checkEncounterEnd on an already-ended encounter is a safe no-op.

EncounterEndedEvent fires exactly once in the encounter's lifetime. Late-joiners reconnecting after end do NOT receive a synthetic EncounterEndedEvent in stream replay (they get the terminal-mode projection in the snapshot — see api pat-v2-terminal-encounter-state for the wire contract).

When adding a new predicate type: extend checkEncounterEnd's body with the new condition (or refactor to a strategy/predicate parameter if the variation grows beyond ~3 cases). Don't move the publish-side effects out — keep ModeEnded transition + event fire colocated with the predicate that triggered it.

Cross-link: api-side pat-v2-terminal-encounter-state (handler-level enforcement) and pat-v2-translator-broadcast-event (wire projection of EncounterEndedEvent)."

      "id": "pat-encounter-player-death-partial",

      "details": "Implementation reality from Wave 2.10 (rpg-toolkit PR #643). The death detection in HP-mutating verbs is asymmetric for players vs monsters:

  - Monster death (TakeAction → player attacks goblin → goblin.HP hits 0): `killEntity(goblinID, playerID)` called → EntityDied + delete + Initiative splice + EntityRemoved + checkEncounterEnd. Full sequence.
  - Player death (NPCAct → goblin attacks alice → alice.HP hits 0): `EntityDiedEvent` fires (with goblin as killerID) for narrative/log/animation purposes, but `killEntity` is NOT called. No EntityRemoved, no Initiative splice, no checkEncounterEnd. Alice stays in the entity table, stays in initiative, stays in turn order.

Why: player dying-state (death saves, going-down/going-up cycle, party rescue) is Wave 2.11+ scope. Wave 2.10 didn't ship the dying-state machine. Removing players on death would have been wrong for that future model — death saves require the player to still be a tracked entity. Firing only EntityDied lets future waves layer dying-state on top without revisiting the death detection.

Death detection is gated on the >0 → 0 HP TRANSITION, not on absolute HP == 0. Caught by Copilot during PR #643 review: the naive check `if entity.HP <= 0 → trigger death` would re-trigger every turn for an already-dead player (alice at 0 HP, bob hits her for 0 damage — current HP is still 0 → no transition → no re-trigger). The correct guard captures pre-mutation HP and checks the transition:

  prevHP := entity.HP
  entity.HP -= damage
  if prevHP > 0 && entity.HP <= 0 {
      // first time crossing zero this turn → fire death detection
  }

Without this guard, an already-dead player would fire repeated EntityDiedEvent and (if Wave 2.11+ wires player killEntity) repeated kill sequences. Same guard applies to monsters but is academic since monsters get fully removed on first hit — the ordering is load-bearing for player-side machinery.

text:
# RPG Toolkit

rpg-toolkit is the rules engine for D&D 5e (and future rulebooks). It implements
game rules and returns rich breakdowns. Consumed by rpg-api (the game server) and
any other rulebook host. The toolkit never orchestrates data, never persists state,
and never imports rpg-api or rpg-api-protos.

## Where things live

- `docs/architecture/overview.md` — layer rules (Core → Events → Mechanics → Tools → Rulebooks), module map, boundary with rpg-api, named violations
- `docs/architecture/data-model.md` — ToData/LoadFromData pattern, entity shapes, chain/breakdown output
- `docs/architecture/components/` — one doc per major module (core, events, dice, mechanics, tools-spatial, tools-environments, tools-spawn, rulebook-dnd5e, refs, items)
- `docs/status.md` — current health: active work, paused items, known rough edges, per-subsystem confidence
- `docs/quality.md` — A-D scorecard with rationale per module
- `docs/adr/` — architectural decisions (32 ADRs). New decisions add new ADRs; superseded ones stay with a "Superseded by ADR-NNN" note. Never archive an ADR.
- `docs/journey/` — exploration narratives (49 docs). How the engine got to where it is. Future contributors learn the engine from these. Do not archive.
- `docs/plans/` — design explorations for specific features (10 plans). Historical; some are implemented, some stale.
- `docs/ideas/` — cross-repo design work scoped to toolkit (3 ideas: action-economy-history, monster-behavior, type-safe-refs).
- `docs/how-to/` — task guides: run-tests, add-a-mechanic, add-a-rulebook-entry, fix-go-mod-replace-directives, verified-transcripts (show a module working as designed: `./scripts/verify.sh <module>`)
- `docs/archive/` — genuine archive: pre-Dec-2025 design docs, diagrams, guides that no longer reflect current architecture. Read for historical context only.

## RPG Toolkit Development Guidelines

## Slash Commands for Common Workflows

Use these slash commands to follow structured workflows:

- `/bugfix` - Complete bug fix workflow (branch creation, failing test, fix, PR)
- `/feature` - Feature development workflow (TDD, implementation, documentation, PR)

These commands guide you through best practices and ensure nothing is missed.

## Module Development Workflow

**IMPORTANT: NO go.work FILES OR LOCAL REPLACE DIRECTIVES**

This project uses a clean module development approach:

1. **Each module is developed independently**
   - Work on one module at a time
   - Use published dependencies only
   - No replace directives pointing to local paths
   - No go.work files

2. **Dependency Management**
   - Modules reference published versions (e.g., `v0.1.0`)
   - When you need updates from another module:
     - Push the changes to that module first
     - Then `go get -u` in the dependent module
   - During development, Go creates pseudo-versions automatically (e.g., `v0.0.0-20230907052031-37f5183ecf93`)

3. **Why This Approach**
   - Keeps development honest - you work with real APIs
   - Focuses work on one module at a time
   - Avoids local development issues and CI failures
   - Clear dependency tracking
   - No confusion about which version is being used

## Testing Strategy

### Preferred Testing Approach: Testify Suite Pattern

**Use testify suite for clean test organization**:

```go
type ServiceTestSuite struct {
    suite.Suite
    service  *Service
    mockDep  *MockDependency
    testData *TestData
}

// SetupTest runs before EACH test function
func (s *ServiceTestSuite) SetupTest() {
    // Create mocks - fresh for each test
    s.mockDep = NewMockDependency(s.T())
    s.service = NewService(&ServiceConfig{
        Dependency: s.mockDep,
    })
    // Initialize common test data
    s.testData = createTestData()
}

// SetupSubTest runs before EACH s.Run()
func (s *ServiceTestSuite) SetupSubTest() {

// Data struct for serialization - uses core.Ref for routing

    Ref               core.Ref `json:"ref"`
    CharacterID       string   `json:"character_id"`
    DamageBonus       int      `json:"damage_bonus"`
    // ... other fields
}

// Runtime struct - no JSON tags needed
type RagingCondition struct {
    CharacterID string
    DamageBonus int
    // ... other fields + non-serialized runtime state
}

// ToJSON serializes to typed struct
func (r *RagingCondition) ToJSON() (json.RawMessage, error) {
    data := RagingData{
        Ref: core.Ref{Module: "dnd5e", Type: "conditions", Value: "raging"},
        CharacterID: r.CharacterID,
        // ...
    }
    return json.Marshal(data)
}

// loadJSON deserializes from typed struct
func (r *RagingCondition) loadJSON(data json.RawMessage) error {
    var ragingData RagingData
    if err := json.Unmarshal(data, &ragingData); err != nil {

    r.CharacterID = ragingData.CharacterID
    // ...
    return nil
}
```

```go
func LoadJSON(data json.RawMessage) (ConditionBehavior, error) {
    var peek struct { Ref core.Ref `json:"ref"` }
    json.Unmarshal(data, &peek)

    switch peek.Ref.Value {
    case "raging":
        c := &RagingCondition{}
        c.loadJSON(data)
        return c, nil
    // ...
    }
}
```

- Type-safe serialization (not `map[string]interface{}`)

// Returns ErrEmptyTable if the table contains no items

func (t *BasicTable[T]) SelectMany(ctx SelectionContext, count int) ([]T, error) {

gl                            # Pull latest changes
gcb fix/issue-number          # Create new feature branch
# ... make changes, run tests ...
git add .
git commit -m "Description"
git push -u origin fix/issue-number
gh pr create                  # Create PR
```

**Development checklist:**
1. Always check existing patterns in similar modules
2. Read Journey and ADR docs before implementing new features
3. Never create files unless necessary - prefer editing existing ones
4. Run the full test suite before committing (`go test ./...`)
5. Run linter before committing (`golangci-lint run ./...`)
6. **Run `go fmt ./...` and `go mod tidy` before committing** - CI checks for diffs
7. Use `gh pr create` for PRs with proper formatting

### Critical Module Isolation Rules
**LEARNED FROM PR #76 TROUBLESHOOTING**

1. **NEVER touch other modules when working on a specific module**
   - Other modules are READ-ONLY for reference
   - If other modules have issues, create separate PRs
   - Don't run `go mod tidy` or similar commands in other modules

2. **Be extremely careful with troubleshooting commands**
   - Always check current directory before running go commands
   - Don't run bulk operations across all modules unless absolutely necessary
   - Accidental `go mod tidy` in wrong modules can corrupt dependencies

3. **Focus on actual changes, not CI configuration**
   - When CI fails, check what files were actually changed first
   - Don't assume CI configuration issues - often it's code conflicts
   - Look for accidentally committed files (like stray modules without go.mod)

4. **Type conflicts from orphaned modules**
   - Files without go.mod get treated as part of root workspace
   - Can cause type conflicts with existing modules
   - Always ensure new modules have proper go.mod or remove them entirely

## AI Assistant Guidelines

**CRITICAL: NO ASSUMPTIONS WITHOUT VERIFICATION**

1. **Research Before Acting**
   - Never make assumptions about tool versions, compatibility, or technical specifications
   - Always research and verify facts before providing commands or instructions
   - Use web search, documentation, or other verification methods when uncertain

2. **Explicit Assumption Declaration**
   - If you must make an assumption, explicitly state: "I'm making an assumption here that..."
   - Explain what you're assuming and why
   - Suggest verification steps the user can take

3. **Version Compatibility**
   - Always check actual compatibility matrices for tools and dependencies
   - Don't assume version support without verification
   - When in doubt, recommend checking official documentation

4. **Error Recovery**
   - When corrected, acknowledge the mistake clearly
   - Update long-term memory (this file) with correct information
   - Learn from the correction to avoid similar errors

5. **Context Disambiguation**
   - **CRITICAL**: This project uses two different "context" concepts
   - **Go Context**: Standard `context.Context` for cancellation, timeouts, request-scoped values
   - **Event Context**: Custom `events.Context` for game data (damage, modifiers, entities)
   - Always specify which context you're referring to
   - Use Go context only where cancellation/timeouts are genuinely needed
   - Remove unused Go context parameters from internal functions
   - Use event context for game data flow between event handlers

## CI Protection Guidelines

**CRITICAL: ALL PUBLIC APIS MUST BE DOCUMENTED**

Follow these patterns to avoid CI failures:

### Documentation Requirements
1. **All Public Functions** must have comments explaining what they do:
   ```go
   // NewBasicTable creates a new weighted selection table with the specified configuration
   func NewBasicTable[T any](config BasicTableConfig) *BasicTable[T] {
   ```

2. **All Public Types** must have comments explaining their purpose:
   ```go
   // SelectionTable provides weighted random selection for any content type
   // Purpose: Core interface for all grabbag/loot table functionality
   type SelectionTable[T any] interface {
   ```

3. **All Public Constants** must have comments explaining their meaning:
   ```go
   // SelectionModeUnique prevents duplicate selections in multi-item rolls
   const SelectionModeUnique SelectionMode = "unique"
   ```

4. **All Public Variables** must have comments explaining their purpose:
   ```go
   // ErrEmptyTable indicates an attempt to select from a table with no items
   var ErrEmptyTable = errors.New("selection table contains no items")
   ```

### Documentation Patterns from Environments Package
Based on `/home/frank/projects/rpg-toolkit/tools/environments/`:

1. **Multi-line purpose explanations**:
   ```go
   // ConstraintType categorizes different kinds of generation constraints
   // Purpose: Allows the generator to handle different constraint types appropriately.
   // Some constraints affect placement, others affect connections, etc.
   type ConstraintType int
   ```

2. **Constructor functions**:
   ```go
   // NewBasicEnvironment creates a new environment with the specified configuration
   // Purpose: Standard constructor with config struct, proper initialization
   func NewBasicEnvironment(config BasicEnvironmentConfig) *BasicEnvironment {
   ```

3. **Interface method documentation**:
   ```go
   // GetID returns the unique identifier for this environment
   func (e *BasicEnvironment) GetID() string {
   
   // SetTheme changes the visual and atmospheric theme of the environment.
   // Purpose: Allows dynamic environment appearance changes during gameplay
   func (e *BasicEnvironment) SetTheme(theme string) error {
   ```

### Implementation Rules
1. **NO functions that only return nil** - CI will fail
2. **NO empty function bodies** - implement meaningful functionality or document why it's intentionally empty
3. **ALL public methods** must have accompanying comments
4. **Follow toolkit naming patterns** - see existing code for conventions

### Error Handling Patterns
```go
// SelectMany selects multiple items from the table with the specified count
// Returns ErrEmptyTable if the table contains no items
// Returns ErrInvalidCount if count is less than 1
func (t *BasicTable[T]) SelectMany(ctx SelectionContext, count int) ([]T, error) {
    if len(t.items) == 0 {
        return nil, ErrEmptyTable
    }
    if count < 1 {
        return nil, ErrInvalidCount
    }
    // ... implementation
}
```

### Pre-Implementation Checklist
Before writing any public API:
1. ✅ Function/type has descriptive comment
2. ✅ Comment explains purpose and behavior  
3. ✅ Error cases documented in comment
4. ✅ Function has meaningful implementation (not just `return nil`)
5. ✅ Follows existing toolkit patterns

# Active handoff — 2026-08-10

## Now

Wave 0 is LIVE VERIFIED. Wave 1 (#180) is exploratory semantic-scope work; implementation has not started.

## Solid

- Wave 0 delivered the Go proto contract as generated root `v0.1.120` / `ba7eda1f1833`, toolkit `encounter/v0.49.1`, and rpg-api#771; verification is recorded on [#192](https://github.com/KirkDiggler/rpg-project/issues/192#issuecomment-5206548237).
- Wave 1 runs structurally usable scope graphs without archetype cardinality/content/spawn enforcement. Missing semantic conventions are follow-up findings only where an existing surface permits; no diagnostics proto/API is added.
- rpg-api-protos#210 is a separate TypeScript/GitHub Release publication defect, not a Go gate. #772 (API update durability) and #885 (toolkit documentation) are separate.

## Next

Focused consistency review of PR #200; the prior independent review is invalidated. Do not cut Wave 1 implementation issues until this course correction is accepted.

## Pointers

- [#180](https://github.com/KirkDiggler/rpg-project/issues/180) · [PR #200](https://github.com/KirkDiggler/rpg-project/pull/200) · [#192 verification](https://github.com/KirkDiggler/rpg-project/issues/192#issuecomment-5206548237) · [rpg-api-protos#210](https://github.com/KirkDiggler/rpg-api-protos/issues/210)

## Lane: encounter reset (play/ family)

**Shipped through 2026-08-11:** `play/{clock,intel,record,interrupt}` all v0.1.0 merged+tagged (docs PRs #906/#911/#912 merged as ratification; journey 052 = bus keeps observation, discovery moves to enumeration). Spatial maintenance shipped by Platform (`tools/spatial/v0.9.0`). **The composition is live: `rulebooks/dnd5e/encounter` v0.1.0** (toolkit #921 merged+tagged 2026-08-11; triplet #918 merged; own module, laws C1–C8, tomb-watch scene, verified-transcript pattern + freeroam workbench + generic `scripts/verify.sh`).

**Wave 2 BUILT, awaiting Kirk:** toolkit [PR #924](https://github.com/KirkDiggler/rpg-toolkit/pull/924) — room-to-room traversal (#922), **CI GREEN**, awaiting merge + tag `rulebooks/dnd5e/encounter/v0.2.0`. Delivers: connection endpoints (nine-defect validation both seams), per-room `GridShape` (hex first-class — answers Platform's square-grid pushback; spatial's bounded HexGrid validity ≡ square's, gridless is the discriminating signal), the `Traverse` verb (TransitionEntity+PlaceEntity, limbo window proven unreachable under four documented invariants), `Decide(Snapshot{Room,Position,Holdings})` + `IntentTraverse` (pursuit through doorways; found+fixed a REAL Pump aliasing bug — planned list held member value copies), the vault-chase scene, `Example_theTraverse`, two-room workbench. 259 tests; 2 sonnet + 2 Opus review rounds, ~50 mutants/probes; `gorelease` verdict = v0.2.0 exactly (one ratified breaking change: Decider interface). Triplet [PR #923](https://github.com/KirkDiggler/rpg-toolkit/pull/923) open with full execution addenda — merges as ratification. Newly pinned laws: full-tick-then-evaluate closure; ending eval is decision-order across actions / declaration-order within one; reject-never-crash covers reentrant deciders. Follow-up noted (not filed): intel `Refreshed` delta ordering nondeterministic (never observable in blobs/transcripts).

**Wiring handed to Platform:** rpg-api [#793](https://github.com/KirkDiggler/rpg-api/issues/793) — free-roam composition as a coexisting encounter type. Kirk's target refinement ON the issue: acceptance = the LOCAL dev loop (#791 override + sandboxseed), `main` stays deployed/frozen, dev may break; no parity (no doors), no dungeon-builder coupling (0.4 unverified / 0.3 unplayable), minimal direct spec; zero proto changes expected (v1alpha2 `EncounterMode.FREE_ROAM` already live; wire hex + per-hex VISIBLE/REMEMBERED ≅ intel ghosts). Local-override allowlist needs a `rulebooks/dnd5e/encounter` target. Depends on the v0.2.0 tag for multi-room.

**Next:** after Kirk merges #924 (+tag) and #923 — the resolution axis, toolkit [#916](https://github.com/KirkDiggler/rpg-toolkit/issues/916) (suspendable MOVEMENT + OA-with-option via play/interrupt; design-first). Kirk's words: "if I have fable, we should do the hard things" — read as ours now, originally routed Platform; confirm at pickup. Combat wave (encounter chaining) rides it. Monster-behavior contributor loop: buddy's ooze (damage slice {dice,type}) rides the decider seam; onboarding docs PR #920 in flight (another session).

Deep record: toolkit `docs/ideas/encounter-transitions/` (the wave-2 triplet + addenda), `docs/ideas/encounter/`, `docs/journey/051+052`.

Wave 2 of the free-roam composition: the declared room topology gets teeth, and pursuit survives doorways.

## What this delivers

- **Connections gain endpoints** (`ConnectionInput.FromPosition/ToPosition`) with a nine-defect validation matrix at both seams (Setup + Load), sorted persistence, and one-defect rejection fixtures with discriminating fragments. New sentinel `ErrBadConnection` (declaration defects).
- **Rooms choose their grid** — `RoomInput.Grid spatial.GridShape` (zero value square: existing blobs and goldens byte-stable; hex first-class per Platform's ask on rpg-api#793). All bounds validity defers to the constructed grid; the module owns no rectangle math. Room-ID validation added (empty/duplicate).
- **The `Traverse` verb** — a member standing at a connection's endpoint crosses to the far endpoint (bidirectional). Module prechecks carry the error contract (`ErrNoConnection` for runtime lookup miss, `ErrBadPlacement` off-threshold); spatial's `TransitionEntity` + `PlaceEntity` execute it with an independently-verified backstop. Percepts refresh both rooms in one pass; sight never crosses an opening; ending evaluation runs at arrival; the clock is untouched (traversal is an activity, not time).
- **Deciders learn where they stand** — `Decide(Snapshot{Room, Position, Holdings})` (the one intentional breaking change, ratified in the design; zero external consumers) plus `IntentTraverse`, executed by Pump in decision order through a shared helper. A REAL latent bug found and fixed en route: Pump's planned list stored member value copies — fatal once traverses mutate `member.Room` — now live-pointer lookups, with the regression pinned. `PumpOutput.MonsterTraverses` mirrors `MonsterMoves`.
- **The vault chase** — a continuous two-room scene: sight, the slip, the ghost pinned at the true last-seen threshold, mid-chase save/reload with the decider re-attached, the goblin's own decision carrying it through the gate, Current reacquired, the ending, and an exact ordered transcript pin.
- **Verified transcript + workbench**: `Example_theTraverse` with a pinned `// Output:`; the freeroam workbench gains a second room and a `traverse` command with room-aware world/belief grids.

## Review rigor

Every task passed a sonnet combined review; Tasks 1 and 3+4 additionally passed Opus deep passes. All findings closed with per-mutant kill evidence (~50 mutants and hostile-blob probes across the wave). Laws newly pinned: full-tick-then-evaluate closure; ending evaluation is decision-order-across-actions, declaration-order within one action; reject-never-crash extended to contract-violating reentrant deciders. R5 limbo-window analysis: unreachable under four documented invariants (comment at the shared seam).

## Compatibility

`gorelease -base v0.1.0`: one incompatible change (`Decider.Decide` signature — the ratified Snapshot migration), all else additive. Suggested version confirmed: **v0.2.0**.

After merge, tag: `rulebooks/dnd5e/encounter/v0.2.0` — this is Platform's dependency signal on rpg-api#793 (multi-room + hex both real).

{"author":{"id":"MDQ6VXNlcjMwMjAxNw==","is_bot":false,"login":"KirkDiggler","name":"Kirk "},"body":"## Goal

Give the composition's declared room topology teeth: traversal through connections, so members — and pursuing monsters — move room to room. Tag as `rulebooks/dnd5e/encounter/v0.2.0`.

## Why now

rpg-api#793 wires the free-roam composition into the game as a coexisting encounter type. The wire is dungeon-absolute and pathing crosses rooms; the composition's `Move` is same-room by documented v1 constraint, and wave 1's `ConnectionInput{ID, From, To}` is declared but inert. Multi-room free roam blocks on this.

## Scope

- `ConnectionInput` gains endpoint positions (the cell each side of the opening occupies); validation + persistence + load rejections in the family's one-defect fixture style.
- An explicit `Traverse` verb (member standing at an endpoint crosses to the far endpoint); ending evaluation runs on arrival; a `traversed` record beat.
- Decider input becomes a snapshot carrying own room + position alongside holdings — resolving the View own-placement gap noted at wave-1 ratification — and the intent vocabulary gains `IntentTraverse`, executed by `Pump`, so pursuit survives doorways.
- Openings only: no door state, no locks, no Interact — deferred by Kirk's call ("we can get there when we get there"). Sight stays room-scoped; connections do not transmit line of sight in this version.

## Out of scope

Door state/locks, cross-room line of sight, combat chaining (rides #916), any dungeon-builder spec coupling.

— asset-pipeline agent, on behalf of KirkDiggler

text:
{"author":{"id":"MDQ6VXNlcjMwMjAxNw==","is_bot":false,"login":"KirkDiggler","name":"Kirk "},"body":"## Goal

Wire the new free-roam encounter composition (`rulebooks/dnd5e/encounter`, v0.1.0 tagged 2026-08-11) into rpg-api as a **coexisting** encounter type — without changing the behavior of any existing dungeon or the old `encounter`-module path.

## Why now, and why no proto work

The wire contract is already ahead of the server: `dnd5e.api.v1alpha2.encounter` carries `EncounterMode.FREE_ROAM` in production, and the verbs wave 1 needs exist (`MoveEntity`, `Interact`, `GetEncounter`, `StreamEncounter`; `TakeAction` already rejects outside TURN_BASED with `FailedPrecondition`). Expected proto delta: **none** (additive-only if projection genuinely demands it; no version bump, `buf breaking` stays green).

## Scope (wave 1 — free-roam only)

- A **third dungeon-key track** in lobby `StartEncounter`: keys resolving to a new-style spec create an encounter backed by `rulebooks/dnd5e/encounter` (`NewEncounter`), persisted as its own aggregate blob with a type discriminator so both encounter types coexist at the repository layer.
- Verb wiring for the new type: `MoveEntity` → `Move` (+ `Pump`); `GetEncounter`/`StreamEncounter` → per-observer `View` projected into the existing per-hex VISIBLE/REMEMBERED knowledge records. Toolkit rooms → dungeon-absolute wire coordinates stay a projection-layer responsibility (the server keeps owning stitching and pathing; room-to-room paths decompose at the adapter).
- **Monster deciders attached at load** — deciders are behavior, never persisted. This is the seam where monster-behavior contributions plug in.
- Tick advancement strictly **RPC-driven** (pump on player activity plus the connect-time self-heal seam); no background loops, no clocks.
- Dev-gated dungeon key(s) so production is untouched.

text:
--- root CLAUDE ---
# RPG Toolkit

rpg-toolkit is the rules engine for D&D 5e (and future rulebooks). It implements
game rules and returns rich breakdowns. Consumed by rpg-api (the game server) and
any other rulebook host. The toolkit never orchestrates data, never persists state,
and never imports rpg-api or rpg-api-protos.

## Where things live

- `docs/architecture/overview.md` — layer rules (Core → Events → Mechanics → Tools → Rulebooks), module map, boundary with rpg-api, named violations
- `docs/architecture/data-model.md` — ToData/LoadFromData pattern, entity shapes, chain/breakdown output
- `docs/architecture/components/` — one doc per major module (core, events, dice, mechanics, tools-spatial, tools-environments, tools-spawn, rulebook-dnd5e, refs, items)
- `docs/status.md` — current health: active work, paused items, known rough edges, per-subsystem confidence
- `docs/quality.md` — A-D scorecard with rationale per module
- `docs/adr/` — architectural decisions (32 ADRs). New decisions add new ADRs; superseded ones stay with a "Superseded by ADR-NNN" note. Never archive an ADR.
- `docs/journey/` — exploration narratives (49 docs). How the engine got to where it is. Future contributors learn the engine from these. Do not archive.
- `docs/plans/` — design explorations for specific features (10 plans). Historical; some are implemented, some stale.
- `docs/ideas/` — cross-repo design work scoped to toolkit (3 ideas: action-economy-history, monster-behavior, type-safe-refs).
- `docs/how-to/` — task guides: run-tests, add-a-mechanic, add-a-rulebook-entry, fix-go-mod-replace-directives, verified-transcripts (show a module working as designed: `./scripts/verify.sh <module>`)
- `docs/archive/` — genuine archive: pre-Dec-2025 design docs, diagrams, guides that no longer reflect current architecture. Read for historical context only.

## RPG Toolkit Development Guidelines

## Slash Commands for Common Workflows

Use these slash commands to follow structured workflows:

- `/bugfix` - Complete bug fix workflow (branch creation, failing test, fix, PR)
- `/feature` - Feature development workflow (TDD, implementation, documentation, PR)

These commands guide you through best practices and ensure nothing is missed.

## Module Development Workflow

**IMPORTANT: NO go.work FILES OR LOCAL REPLACE DIRECTIVES**

This project uses a clean module development approach:

1. **Each module is developed independently**
   - Work on one module at a time
   - Use published dependencies only
   - No replace directives pointing to local paths
   - No go.work files

2. **Dependency Management**
   - Modules reference published versions (e.g., `v0.1.0`)
   - When you need updates from another module:
     - Push the changes to that module first
     - Then `go get -u` in the dependent module
   - During development, Go creates pseudo-versions automatically (e.g., `v0.0.0-20230907052031-37f5183ecf93`)

3. **Why This Approach**
   - Keeps development honest - you work with real APIs
   - Focuses work on one module at a time
   - Avoids local development issues and CI failures
   - Clear dependency tracking
   - No confusion about which version is being used

## Testing Strategy

### Preferred Testing Approach: Testify Suite Pattern

**Use testify suite for clean test organization**:

```go
type ServiceTestSuite struct {
    suite.Suite
    service  *Service
    mockDep  *MockDependency
    testData *TestData
}

// SetupTest runs before EACH test function
func (s *ServiceTestSuite) SetupTest() {
    // Create mocks - fresh for each test
    s.mockDep = NewMockDependency(s.T())
    s.service = NewService(&ServiceConfig{
        Dependency: s.mockDep,
    })
    // Initialize common test data
    s.testData = createTestData()
}

// SetupSubTest runs before EACH s.Run()
func (s *ServiceTestSuite) SetupSubTest() {
    // Reset test data to clean state for each subtest
    s.testData = createTestData()
    // Can also reset specific mock expectations if needed
}

// Run the suite
func TestServiceSuite(t *testing.T) {
    suite.Run(t, new(ServiceTestSuite))
}
```

**Key Testing Principles**:
- Use `suite.Suite` for test organization
- Use `s.Run()` for subtests with test cases
- `SetupTest()` runs before each test function - establish mocks here
- `SetupSubTest()` runs before each `s.Run()` - reset test data here
- Keep test bodies focused on arrange/act/assert
- Use suite assertions: `s.Assert()`, `s.Require()`

### Testing Commands

When working on a module:
```bash
# Run tests
go test ./...

# Run linter
golangci-lint run ./...

# Update dependencies
go get -u ./...
go mod tidy
```

## Pre-commit Checks

The repository has comprehensive pre-commit hooks that run:
- Formatting (gofmt, goimports)
- go mod tidy
- Linting
- Tests

These run automatically on commit.

## Development Principles

- **Optimize for simplicity, not hypothetical future needs**
- **Only add what is necessary**
- **Pick ONE way to represent data and use it directly**
- **Avoid conversion layers and dual representations**
- **Delete code that creates unnecessary indirection**

## Project Philosophy

**IMPORTANT: RPG Toolkit provides infrastructure, NOT implementation**

1. **Generic Tools, Not Game Rules**
   - We provide the infrastructure for game mechanics
   - Games implement their specific rules using our tools
   - Example: We provide proficiency infrastructure, games define what "Acrobatics" means

2. **Event-Driven Architecture**
   - Modules communicate through events, not direct calls
   - Use the event bus for all inter-module communication
   - This allows maximum flexibility for game implementations

3. **Entity-Based Design**
   - All game objects implement core.Entity interface
   - Entities have ID and Type
   - This provides consistent patterns across the toolkit

## Current Project Status

### Completed Modules
1. **core** - Base interfaces and types
2. **events** - Event bus system for module communication
3. **dice** - Dice rolling infrastructure
4. **mechanics/conditions** - Status effects and conditions
5. **mechanics/proficiency** - Proficiency system
6. **mechanics/effects** - Shared infrastructure for conditions/proficiencies
7. **mechanics/resources** - Resource management (spell slots, abilities, etc.)
8. **tools/spatial** - Complete spatial positioning system with multi-room orchestration
9. **tools/spawn** - Complete entity spawn engine with Phases 1-4 implementation per ADR-0013

### Spatial Module Features (Completed)
- **Grid Systems**: Square (D&D 5e), Hex, and Gridless positioning
- **Room Management**: Entity placement, movement, and spatial queries
- **Multi-Room Orchestration**: Connection system, layout patterns, entity transitions
- **Event Integration**: Full event-driven architecture
- **Query System**: Efficient spatial queries with filtering
- **Connection Types**: Doors, stairs, passages, portals, bridges, tunnels
- **Layout Patterns**: Tower, branching, grid, and organic arrangements

### Pending Work (Issues #31-#33)
1. **Equipment System (#31)** - Items, inventory, equip/unequip mechanics
2. **Enhanced Conditions (#32)** - Advanced condition features
3. **Feature System (#33)** - Character features and traits

### Important Patterns
1. **Config Pattern**: Use config structs for constructors
2. **Composition Over Inheritance**: Use embedded structs and interfaces
3. **Error Handling**: Always check errors in tests with require.NoError(t, err)
4. **Event Naming**: Use dot notation (e.g., "resource.consumed", "condition.applied")
5. **Typed Constants Pattern**: See below
6. **JSON Serialization Pattern**: See below

### Typed Constants Pattern

**Toolkit is the source of truth for game mechanics identifiers.**

Game server (rpg-api) is a pure translator:

**IMPORTANT: Typed Data Structs for JSON**

Features and Conditions use a JSON-in/JSON-out pattern where:

    Ref               core.Ref `json:"ref"`
    CharacterID       string   `json:"character_id"`
    DamageBonus       int      `json:"damage_bonus"`
    // ... other fields
}

// Runtime struct - no JSON tags needed
type RagingCondition struct {
    CharacterID string
    DamageBonus int
    // ... other fields + non-serialized runtime state
}

// ToJSON serializes to typed struct
func (r *RagingCondition) ToJSON() (json.RawMessage, error) {
    data := RagingData{
        Ref: core.Ref{Module: "dnd5e", Type: "conditions", Value: "raging"},
        CharacterID: r.CharacterID,
        // ...
    }
    return json.Marshal(data)
}

// loadJSON deserializes from typed struct
func (r *RagingCondition) loadJSON(data json.RawMessage) error {
    var ragingData RagingData
    if err := json.Unmarshal(data, &ragingData); err != nil {
        return err
    }
    r.CharacterID = ragingData.CharacterID
    // ...
    return nil
}
```

**Loader routes by ref:**
```go
func LoadJSON(data json.RawMessage) (ConditionBehavior, error) {
    var peek struct { Ref core.Ref `json:"ref"` }
    json.Unmarshal(data, &peek)

    switch peek.Ref.Value {
    case "raging":
        c := &RagingCondition{}
        c.loadJSON(data)
        return c, nil
    // ...
    }
}
```

- Type-safe serialization (not `map[string]interface{}`)

- Game server doesn't need to understand toolkit internals

# D&D 5e Rulebook Development Guidelines

This document contains patterns specific to the dnd5e rulebook module.

## Refs Pattern

**Everything has a Ref.** All identifiable content (features, conditions, combat abilities, actions, weapons, etc.) must have a `*core.Ref` with `{Module, Type, ID}`.

- Module: `"dnd5e"` (enables future modules like `"artificer"` without ID conflicts)
- Type: Category (`"features"`, `"conditions"`, `"actions"`, etc.)
- ID: Specific identifier (`"rage"`, `"dodging"`, `"strike"`)

**Game server uses Refs** to identify what to activate/check. Proto enum maps to Ref.

**Loaders reconstitute behavior.** Refs identify the module/package, then:
- `LoadFromData(data)` - When types share a consistent schema (e.g., actions)
- `LoadJSON(data)` - When types have unique state structures (e.g., features, conditions)

Choose based on whether the data structure is homogeneous or heterogeneous.

**Refs namespace pattern** (`refs/` package):
```go
refs.Features.Rage()           // *core.Ref for Rage feature
refs.Conditions.Dodging()      // *core.Ref for Dodging condition
refs.CombatAbilities.Attack()  // *core.Ref for Attack ability
refs.Actions.Strike()          // *core.Ref for Strike action
```

## Conditions vs Effects

Conditions are really "effects" but we're saving that rename for 1.0. Use `character.HasCondition(refs.Conditions.Dodging())` to check for active effects like Dodging or Disengaging.

## Two-Level Action Economy

D&D 5e has two levels of resource consumption:

1. **Action Economy** - What you spend (action, bonus action, reaction)
2. **Capacity** - What you get to do (attacks, movement, off-hand attacks, flurry strikes)

Example: Taking the Attack ability (spends action) grants attacks (capacity). Each Strike action consumes one attack from that capacity.

Key fields in `ActionEconomy`:
- Primary: `ActionsRemaining`, `BonusActionsRemaining`, `ReactionsRemaining`
- Capacity: `AttacksRemaining`, `MovementRemaining`, `OffHandAttacksRemaining`, `FlurryStrikesRemaining`

### Preferred Testing Approach: Testify Suite Pattern

**Use testify suite for clean test organization**:

```go
type ServiceTestSuite struct {
    suite.Suite
    service  *Service
    mockDep  *MockDependency
    testData *TestData
}

// SetupTest runs before EACH test function
func (s *ServiceTestSuite) SetupTest() {
    // Create mocks - fresh for each test
    s.mockDep = NewMockDependency(s.T())
    s.service = NewService(&ServiceConfig{
        Dependency: s.mockDep,
    })
    // Initialize common test data
    s.testData = createTestData()
}

// SetupSubTest runs before EACH s.Run()
func (s *ServiceTestSuite) SetupSubTest() {
    // Reset test data to clean state for each subtest
    s.testData = createTestData()
    // Can also reset specific mock expectations if needed
}

// Run the suite
func TestServiceSuite(t *testing.T) {
    suite.Run(t, new(ServiceTestSuite))
}
```

- Use `suite.Suite` for test organization
- Use `s.Run()` for subtests with test cases
- `SetupTest()` runs before each test function - establish mocks here
- `SetupSubTest()` runs before each `s.Run()` - reset test data here
- Keep test bodies focused on arrange/act/assert
- Use suite assertions: `s.Assert()`, `s.Require()`

- **Delete code that creates unnecessary indirection**

   - Always research and verify facts before providing commands or instructions

2. **Explicit Assumption Declaration**

   - Explain what you're assuming and why

3. **Version Compatibility**
   - Always check actual compatibility matrices for tools and dependencies

   - When in doubt, recommend checking official documentation

4. **Error Recovery**
   - When corrected, acknowledge the mistake clearly

   - **CRITICAL**: This project uses two different "context" concepts

   - Use Go context only where cancellation/timeouts are genuinely needed
   - Remove unused Go context parameters from internal functions

# D&D 5e Rulebook Development Guidelines

This document contains patterns specific to the dnd5e rulebook module.

## Refs Pattern

**Everything has a Ref.** All identifiable content (features, conditions, combat abilities, actions, weapons, etc.) must have a `*core.Ref` with `{Module, Type, ID}`.

- Module: `"dnd5e"` (enables future modules like `"artificer"` without ID conflicts)
- Type: Category (`"features"`, `"conditions"`, `"actions"`, etc.)
- ID: Specific identifier (`"rage"`, `"dodging"`, `"strike"`)

**Game server uses Refs** to identify what to activate/check. Proto enum maps to Ref.

**Loaders reconstitute behavior.** Refs identify the module/package, then:
- `LoadFromData(data)` - When types share a consistent schema (e.g., actions)
- `LoadJSON(data)` - When types have unique state structures (e.g., features, conditions)

Choose based on whether the data structure is homogeneous or heterogeneous.

**Refs namespace pattern** (`refs/` package):
```go
refs.Features.Rage()           // *core.Ref for Rage feature
refs.Conditions.Dodging()      // *core.Ref for Dodging condition
refs.CombatAbilities.Attack()  // *core.Ref for Attack ability
refs.Actions.Strike()          // *core.Ref for Strike action
```

## Conditions vs Effects

Conditions are really "effects" but we're saving that rename for 1.0. Use `character.HasCondition(refs.Conditions.Dodging())` to check for active effects like Dodging or Disengaging.

## Two-Level Action Economy

D&D 5e has two levels of resource consumption:

1. **Action Economy** - What you spend (action, bonus action, reaction)
2. **Capacity** - What you get to do (attacks, movement, off-hand attacks, flurry strikes)

Example: Taking the Attack ability (spends action) grants attacks (capacity). Each Strike action consumes one attack from that capacity.

Key fields in `ActionEconomy`:
- Primary: `ActionsRemaining`, `BonusActionsRemaining`, `ReactionsRemaining`
- Capacity: `AttacksRemaining`, `MovementRemaining`, `OffHandAttacksRemaining`, `FlurryStrikesRemaining`

   117	// ToData returns a persistent snapshot of this Encounter.
   118	// All slices and embedded data are deep-copied; mutating the returned
   119	// EncounterData will not affect this Encounter (snapshot immunity).
   120	func (e *Encounter) ToData() EncounterData {
   121		// Members in sorted-ID order: an unchanged encounter must produce
   122		// byte-identical snapshots (T6 review M1 — map iteration here made
   123		// ToData nondeterministic and the round-trip suite ~16% flaky).
   124		memberIDs := make([]MemberID, 0, len(e.members))
   125		for id := range e.members {
   126			memberIDs = append(memberIDs, id)
   127		}
   128		sort.Slice(memberIDs, func(i, j int) bool { return memberIDs[i] < memberIDs[j] })
   129		membersData := make([]MemberData, 0, len(memberIDs))
   130		for _, id := range memberIDs {
   131			m := e.members[id]
   132			room, ok := e.orchestrator.GetRoom(m.Room)
   133			if !ok {
   134				continue // Room not found (shouldn't happen in valid encounter)
   135			}
   136			pos, ok := room.GetEntityPosition(string(m.ID))
   137			if !ok {
   138				continue // Position not found (shouldn't happen in valid encounter)
   139			}
   140			membersData = append(membersData, MemberData{
   141				ID:       m.ID,
   142				Kind:     m.Kind,
   143				Room:     m.Room,
   144				Position: PositionData{X: pos.X, Y: pos.Y},
   145			})
   146		}
   147	
   148		// Deep-copy endings in declaration order
   149		endingsData := make([]EndingData, len(e.endings))
   150		for i, de := range e.endings {
   151			ed := EndingData{
   152				Key: de.key,
   153			}
   154	
   155			switch t := de.trigger.(type) {
   156			case TriggerReachedPosition:
   157				ed.Kind = "reached_position"
   158				ed.Room = t.Room
   159				ed.Position = &PositionData{X: t.Position.X, Y: t.Position.Y}
   160				ed.Member = t.Member
   161			case TriggerExternal:
   162				ed.Kind = "external"
   163			}
   164	
   165			endingsData[i] = ed
   166		}
   167	
   168		// Deep-copy everMembers in sorted order for determinism
   169		everMembersSlice := make([]MemberID, 0, len(e.everMembers))
   170		for id := range e.everMembers {
   171			everMembersSlice = append(everMembersSlice, id)
   172		}
   173		slices.SortFunc(everMembersSlice, func(a, b MemberID) int {
   174			if a < b {
   175				return -1
   176			}
   177			if a > b {
   178				return 1
   179			}
   180			return 0
   181		})
   182	
   183		// Deep-copy field from stored inputs
   184		fieldData := FieldData{
   185			Rooms:       make([]RoomData, len(e.fieldInput)),
   186			Connections: make([]ConnectionData, len(e.connectionsInput)),
   187		}
   188	
   189		for i, ri := range e.fieldInput {
   190			rd := RoomData{
   191				ID:         ri.ID,
   192				Width:      ri.Width,
   193				Height:     ri.Height,
   194				Grid:       gridShapeToData(ri.Grid),
   195				Occluders:  make([]PositionData, len(ri.Occluders)),
   196				Boundaries: make([]BoundaryData, len(ri.Boundaries)),
   197			}
   198	
   199			for j, occ := range ri.Occluders {
   200				rd.Occluders[j] = PositionData{X: occ.X, Y: occ.Y}
   201			}
   202	
   203			for j, b := range ri.Boundaries {
   204				rd.Boundaries[j] = BoundaryData{
   205					From:              PositionData{X: b.From.X, Y: b.From.Y},
   206					To:                PositionData{X: b.To.X, Y: b.To.Y},
   207					BlocksMovement:    b.BlocksMovement,
   208					BlocksLineOfSight: b.BlocksLineOfSight,
   209				}
   210			}
   211	
   212			fieldData.Rooms[i] = rd
   213		}
   214	
   215		for i, ci := range e.connectionsInput {
   216			fieldData.Connections[i] = ConnectionData{
   217				ID:           ci.ID,
   218				From:         ci.From,
   219				To:           ci.To,
   220				FromPosition: &PositionData{X: ci.FromPosition.X, Y: ci.FromPosition.Y},
   221				ToPosition:   &PositionData{X: ci.ToPosition.X, Y: ci.ToPosition.Y},
   222			}
   223		}
   224	
   225		// Build outcome if present
   226		var outcomeData *OutcomeData
   227		if e.outcome != nil {
   228			outcomeData = &OutcomeData{
   229				Ending:  e.outcome.Ending,
   230				At:      e.outcome.At,
   231				Members: make([]MemberOutcomeData, len(e.outcome.Members)),
   232			}
   233			for i, mo := range e.outcome.Members {
   234				outcomeData.Members[i] = MemberOutcomeData{
   235					ID:       mo.ID,
   236					Room:     mo.Room,
   237					Position: PositionData{X: mo.Position.X, Y: mo.Position.Y},
   238				}
   239			}
   240		}
   241	
   242		return EncounterData{
   243			Outcome:     outcomeData,
   244			Clock:       e.clock.ToData(),
   245			Intel:       e.intelLog.ToData(),
   246			Log:         e.story.ToData(),
   247			Field:       fieldData,
   248			Members:     membersData,
   249			Endings:     endingsData,
   250			EverMembers: everMembersSlice,
   251		}
   252	}

     5

     9	)
    10	
    11	// Intent represents a decision made by a decider in response to their
    12	// Snapshot. The anti-wall-hack contract: a decider receives ONLY its own
    13	// Snapshot (own room, own position, own holdings), never the full
    14	// encounter state or another member's live truth. Intent is a sealed
    15	// type (unexported marker method).
    16	type Intent interface {
    17		isIntent()
    18	}
    19	
    20	// IntentMoveTo represents a decision to move to a specific position.
    21	type IntentMoveTo struct {
    22		// To is the target position the member intends to move to.
    23		To spatial.Position
    24	}
    25	
    26	// isIntent marks IntentMoveTo as an Intent.
    27	func (i IntentMoveTo) isIntent() {}
    28	
    29	// IntentHold represents a decision to stay in place (do nothing this tick).
    30	type IntentHold struct{}
    31	
    32	// isIntent marks IntentHold as an Intent.
    33	func (i IntentHold) isIntent() {}
    34	
    35	// IntentTraverse represents a decision to cross a connection into the room
    36	// on its other side. Preconditions match the Traverse verb exactly: the
    37	// decider's own Snapshot.Room/Position (see Snapshot) must be standing
    38	// exactly on one of the named connection's two endpoints. An illegal
    39	// traverse intent (unknown connection, or not at the threshold) does not
    40	// abort the pump — it follows the same silent-skip contract Pump already
    41	// applies to a spatially-rejected IntentMoveTo: no beat, no room/position
    42	// change for that member, everything else in the pump proceeds normally.
    43	type IntentTraverse struct {
    44		// Connection is the ID of the connection to traverse.
    45		Connection string
    46	}
    47	
    48	// isIntent marks IntentTraverse as an Intent.
    49	func (i IntentTraverse) isIntent() {}
    50	
    51	// Snapshot is a decider's complete input: their OWN current placement
    52	// (room and position) plus their OWN held intel. The anti-wall-hack
    53	// contract (C2) extends to placement, not just holdings — a decider
    54	// learns where IT stands, never where any other member stands except
    55	// through Holdings' sighted percepts. Static field topology (e.g. a
    56	// connections list, for a pursuit decider that needs to know where the
    57	// doors are) is NOT part of Snapshot; give it to a decider at
    58	// construction time instead — Snapshot itself carries only what changes
    59	// tick to tick.
    60	type Snapshot struct {
    61		// Room is the decider's own current room ID.
    62		Room string
    63	
    64		// Position is the decider's own current position within Room.
    65		Position spatial.Position
    66	
    67		// Holdings is the decider's own held intel — exactly what HeldBy
    68		// returns for this member, nothing more (C2).
    69		Holdings []intel.Holding
    70	}
    71	
    72	// Decider is the interface for monster intelligence. A decider receives ONLY
    73	// its own Snapshot (own room, own position, own holdings — never another
    74	// member's live truth) and returns an Intent representing what the monster
    75	// wants to do, or an error that aborts the pump atomically. The anti-wall-
    76	// hack contract is structural: Decide receives exactly what the monster
    77	// knows about itself and can see, nothing more.
    78	type Decider interface {
    79		// Decide takes the decider's own Snapshot and returns an Intent (what
    80		// to do) or an error that aborts the pump atomically. If an error is
    81		// returned, the Pump rolls back completely: the clock is not advanced,
    82		// no moves are executed, and no record beats are appended.
    83		Decide(snap Snapshot) (Intent, error)
    84	}

   117	// ToData returns a persistent snapshot of this Encounter.
   118	// All slices and embedded data are deep-copied; mutating the returned
   119	// EncounterData will not affect this Encounter (snapshot immunity).
   120	func (e *Encounter) ToData() EncounterData {
   121		// Members in sorted-ID order: an unchanged encounter must produce
   122		// byte-identical snapshots (T6 review M1 — map iteration here made
   123		// ToData nondeterministic and the round-trip suite ~16% flaky).
   124		memberIDs := make([]MemberID, 0, len(e.members))
   125		for id := range e.members {
   126			memberIDs = append(memberIDs, id)
   127		}
   128		sort.Slice(memberIDs, func(i, j int) bool { return memberIDs[i] < memberIDs[j] })
   129		membersData := make([]MemberData, 0, len(memberIDs))
   130		for _, id := range memberIDs {
   131			m := e.members[id]
   132			room, ok := e.orchestrator.GetRoom(m.Room)
   133			if !ok {
   134				continue // Room not found (shouldn't happen in valid encounter)
   135			}
   136			pos, ok := room.GetEntityPosition(string(m.ID))
   137			if !ok {
   138				continue // Position not found (shouldn't happen in valid encounter)
   139			}
   140			membersData = append(membersData, MemberData{
   141				ID:       m.ID,
   142				Kind:     m.Kind,
   143				Room:     m.Room,
   144				Position: PositionData{X: pos.X, Y: pos.Y},
   145			})
   146		}
   147	
   148		// Deep-copy endings in declaration order
   149		endingsData := make([]EndingData, len(e.endings))
   150		for i, de := range e.endings {
   151			ed := EndingData{
   152				Key: de.key,
   153			}
   154	
   155			switch t := de.trigger.(type) {
   156			case TriggerReachedPosition:
   157				ed.Kind = "reached_position"
   158				ed.Room = t.Room
   159				ed.Position = &PositionData{X: t.Position.X, Y: t.Position.Y}
   160				ed.Member = t.Member
   161			case TriggerExternal:
   162				ed.Kind = "external"
   163			}

   165			endingsData[i] = ed
   166		}
   167	
   168		// Deep-copy everMembers in sorted order for determinism
   169		everMembersSlice := make([]MemberID, 0, len(e.everMembers))
   170		for id := range e.everMembers {
   171			everMembersSlice = append(everMembersSlice, id)
   172		}
   173		slices.SortFunc(everMembersSlice, func(a, b MemberID) int {
   174			if a < b {
   175				return -1
   176			}
   177			if a > b {
   178				return 1
   179			}
   180			return 0
   181		})
   182	
   183		// Deep-copy field from stored inputs
   184		fieldData := FieldData{
   185			Rooms:       make([]RoomData, len(e.fieldInput)),
   186			Connections: make([]ConnectionData, len(e.connectionsInput)),
   187		}
   188	
   189		for i, ri := range e.fieldInput {
   190			rd := RoomData{
   191				ID:         ri.ID,
   192				Width:      ri.Width,
   193				Height:     ri.Height,
   194				Grid:       gridShapeToData(ri.Grid),
   195				Occluders:  make([]PositionData, len(ri.Occluders)),
   196				Boundaries: make([]BoundaryData, len(ri.Boundaries)),
   197			}
   198	
   199			for j, occ := range ri.Occluders {
   200				rd.Occluders[j] = PositionData{X: occ.X, Y: occ.Y}
   201			}
   202	
   203			for j, b := range ri.Boundaries {
   204				rd.Boundaries[j] = BoundaryData{
   205					From:              PositionData{X: b.From.X, Y: b.From.Y},
   206					To:                PositionData{X: b.To.X, Y: b.To.Y},
   207					BlocksMovement:    b.BlocksMovement,
   208					BlocksLineOfSight: b.BlocksLineOfSight,
   209				}
   210			}
   211	
   212			fieldData.Rooms[i] = rd
   213		}
   214	
   215		for i, ci := range e.connectionsInput {
   216			fieldData.Connections[i] = ConnectionData{
   217				ID:           ci.ID,
   218				From:         ci.From,
   219				To:           ci.To,
   220				FromPosition: &PositionData{X: ci.FromPosition.X, Y: ci.FromPosition.Y},
   221				ToPosition:   &PositionData{X: ci.ToPosition.X, Y: ci.ToPosition.Y},
   222			}
   223		}

   228			outcomeData = &OutcomeData{
   229				Ending:  e.outcome.Ending,
   230				At:      e.outcome.At,
   231				Members: make([]MemberOutcomeData, len(e.outcome.Members)),
   232			}

   234				outcomeData.Members[i] = MemberOutcomeData{
   235					ID:       mo.ID,
   236					Room:     mo.Room,
   237					Position: PositionData{X: mo.Position.X, Y: mo.Position.Y},

     1	# Encounter transitions — design (v0.2.0)
     2	
     3	Amends the wave-1 design (`docs/ideas/encounter/design.md`). Everything
     4	not named here carries over unchanged: laws C1–C8, the verb/query
     5	surfaces, persistence-at-the-seam, family signature law, R8/R9
     6	discipline.
     7	
     8	## New laws
     9	
    10	- **T1 — connections are open.** A connection is a bidirectional
    11	  opening between two rooms with exactly one endpoint cell in each. No
    12	  state, no locks, no Interact. Door state is a future wave.
    13	- **T2 — traversal is standing at the threshold.** `Traverse` requires
    14	  the member's position to equal the connection's endpoint in the
    15	  member's current room; the member arrives at the far endpoint in the
    16	  other room. Anything else is `ErrBadPlacement`.
    17	- **T3 — sight never crosses a connection.** Percept computation
    18	  remains room-scoped. An opening is not a window.
    19	- **T4 — traversal is an activity, not time.** Like `Move`, `Traverse`
    20	  never advances the clock. Only `Pump` advances the clock.
    21	- **T5 — deciders know self, holdings, and the map; never live truth.**
    22	  The decide phase receives the decider's own room + position and its
    23	  holdings. Static topology may be given to a decider at construction.
    24	  C2 stands: nothing about other members' current state ever reaches a
    25	  decider except through its own holdings.
    26	
    27	## Type changes
    28	
    29	```go
    30	// RoomInput gains a grid choice. Zero value is GridShapeSquare —
    31	// existing setups, tests, and goldens are untouched. Hex rooms make
    32	// the dungeon-absolute hex wire projection an identity mapping.
    33	type RoomInput struct {
    34		// ... existing fields ...
    35		Grid spatial.GridShape // square (default) | hex | gridless
    36	}
    37	// In-bounds validation (member placement, connection endpoints,
    38	// movement targets) defers to the constructed grid's own validity
    39	// check; the module owns no rectangle math of its own.
    40	
    41	// ConnectionInput gains endpoints (BREAKING for stored v0.1 data that
    42	// declared connections — none exists; rpg-api is not wired yet).
    43	type ConnectionInput struct {
    44		ID string
    45		From string                 // room ID
    46		FromPosition spatial.Position // endpoint cell in From
    47		To string                   // room ID
    48		ToPosition spatial.Position   // endpoint cell in To
    49	}
    50	
    51	// TraverseInput follows the family signature law.
    52	type TraverseInput struct {
    53		Member     MemberID
    54		Connection string // ConnectionInput.ID
    55	}
    56	
    57	// TraverseOutput mirrors MoveOutput: deltas, never published; Outcome
    58	// present iff the arrival closed the encounter.
    59	type TraverseOutput struct { /* same shape family as MoveOutput */ }
    60	
    61	// Snapshot is what a decider decides from. Replaces the bare holdings
    62	// slice (interface change; zero external implementors).
    63	type Snapshot struct {
    64		Room     string
    65		Position spatial.Position
    66		Holdings []intel.Holding
    67	}
    68	
    69	type Decider interface {
    70		Decide(snap Snapshot) (Intent, error)
    71	}
    72	
    73	// IntentTraverse joins IntentMoveTo and IntentHold.
    74	type IntentTraverse struct {
    75		Connection string
    76	}
    77	```

    79	## Verb surface
    80	
    81	| Verb | Change |
    82	|---|---|
    83	| `Traverse(*TraverseInput) (*TraverseOutput, error)` | NEW. Precondition per T2. Refreshes percepts in **both** rooms (departure and arrival are observable absences/appearances). Appends a `traversed` beat. Runs ending evaluation at the arrival position. Rejects on `ErrClosed`, `ErrNilInput`, `ErrNoMember`, `ErrNoConnection`, `ErrBadPlacement`. |
    84	| `Move` | Unchanged, still same-room; its doc comment stays honest about that. |
    85	| `Pump` | Phase 2 executes `IntentTraverse` with the same T2 precondition. Failure contract (corrected during Task 3 to match the module's shipped v0.1 semantics): a phase-1 decider ERROR aborts the pump atomically (R5 — clock untouched, no beats, nothing executed); a phase-2 EXECUTION failure (illegal position, unknown connection) is silently skipped — the pump completes, and that action is simply absent from output and beats — exactly like a failed `IntentMoveTo` has always behaved. |
    86	| `View`, `Story`, `Join`, `Exit`, `End`, `ToData`/`LoadEncounter` | Unchanged surfaces; behavior notes below. |
    87	
    88	New sentinel: `ErrNoConnection` (unknown connection ID), wrapped
    89	multi-`%w` like the family's other sentinels and pinned by `errors.Is`.
    90	
    91	## Validation (Setup and Load — same rules, one-defect fixtures)
    92	
    93	Reject when: duplicate connection ID; `From`/`To` names an unknown
    94	room; `From == To` (self-connection); an endpoint out of the room's
    95	bounds; an endpoint on an occluder. Load-side violations wrap
    96	`ErrInvalidData` multi-`%w` with discriminating message fragments, in
    97	the wave-1 `validEncounterData()` one-defect table style. Every new
    98	field appears in the rich golden (`TestGoldenJSONRich` grows
    99	connections with both endpoints).
   100	
   101	## Persistence
   102	
   103	`FieldData` already persists construction inputs; connections gain
   104	their endpoint fields in the blob. Reload pins: a member who traversed
   105	reloads in the **new** room (construct-path reload preserves member
   106	room, not connection history); ordered iteration stays deterministic
   107	(C8 — connections sorted by ID wherever order is observable).
   108	
   109	## Decider flow (the point of the wave)
   110	
   111	A goblin standing in the crypt saw alice slip through the north opening
   112	last tick. Its holdings contain a ghost whose `SightPayload.Room` says
   113	`hall`. Constructed with the map, it knows `north-door` leads there. It
   114	decides `IntentTraverse{Connection: "north-door"}`; phase 2 executes;
   115	its percepts refresh in the hall; the chase is on. This must exist as
   116	an integration pin (the wave's vandalDecider analogue): decider crosses
   117	a room boundary in pursuit of a ghost, using only self + holdings + the
   118	map it was built with.
   119	
   120	## Compatibility notes (honest, both acceptable at zero consumers)
   121	
   122	1. Stored v0.1 blobs that declared connections fail v0.2 load
   123	   (endpoints required). No such blobs exist outside this repo's own
   124	   fixtures.
   125	2. `Decider` implementors must adopt `Snapshot`. The only implementors
   126	   live in this module's tests and workbench.
   127	
   128	`gorelease` gate stays in CI; tag `rulebooks/dnd5e/encounter/v0.2.0`.
   129	
   130	Wire-shape amendments (Copilot round on PR #924, ratified): the blob
   131	persists grid shape as a **string** using spatial's own serialization
   132	vocabulary (`GridTypeHex`/`GridTypeGridless`; empty = square), never
   133	the iota integer — constant reordering must not reinterpret stored
   134	data. Connection endpoints persist as pointers with **presence
   135	required at load** (nil → ErrInvalidData+ErrBadConnection naming the
   136	side) — a missing endpoint must reject, not silently become the legal
   137	cell (0,0). This is what makes compat note 1 above genuinely true.
   138	
   139	Coordinate-model amendment (Kirk, 2026-08-11, ratified): **hex rooms
   140	speak axial/cube, not offset.** `buildRoomGrid` constructs spatial's
   141	`AxialHexGrid` — Position.X/Y are axial Q/R (S = -(Q+R) derived);
   142	bounds are origin-centered spans (negative coordinates legal), unlike
   143	square/gridless's (0,0)-origin rectangles; distance/adjacency/LoS run
   144	the pure cube formulas. Why: the wire and server pathing already speak
   145	cube — axial is cube's lossless 2D projection, so the projection at
   146	the seam is an identity, where the previously-chosen offset HexGrid
   147	would have forced a parity-dependent conversion (the exact confusion
   148	Platform flagged). Side effect: hex validity now diverges from
   149	square's, so the hex tests independently kill the build-square-always
   150	mutant (superseding the earlier "only gridless discriminates"
   151	finding).
   152	
   153	## Acceptance criteria
   154	
   155	- A two-room field with one opening validates, round-trips, and
   156	  rejects each defect class individually with the pinned fragment.
   157	- A player at the threshold traverses; away from it, `ErrBadPlacement`;
   158	  unknown connection, `ErrNoConnection`; after close, `ErrClosed` (the
   159	  sweep grows `Traverse`).
   160	- Traversal triggers ending evaluation: arriving on a
   161	  `TriggerReachedPosition` cell in the destination room closes the
   162	  encounter with the declared key.
   163	- A decider-driven monster pursues a ghost through an opening
   164	  (integration pin above); the pump stays atomic when a traverse
   165	  intent's precondition fails.
   166	- Percepts: departure room observers lose Current status on the
   167	  traverser (ghost forms at the threshold); arrival room observers gain
   168	  Current; sight does not cross the opening in either direction (T3
   169	  pin: observer adjacent to an endpoint sees nothing in the far room).
   170	- Scene test tells one continuous story ending in a cross-room event;
   171	  the wave-1 tombwatch scene and its archived transcript stay
   172	  untouched.
   173	- The module Example gains (or a sibling Example adds) a pinned
   174	  transcript showing a traversal beat; `./scripts/verify.sh
   175	  rulebooks/dnd5e/encounter` prints it.

     1	# Encounter transitions — brainstorm (wave 2 of the free-roam composition)
     2	
     3	Issue: #922. Builds on `docs/ideas/encounter/` (wave 1, shipped as
     4	`rulebooks/dnd5e/encounter/v0.1.0`, PR #921). Ratified conversationally
     5	with Kirk on 2026-08-10; this document records the decisions and his
     6	words that shaped them.
     7	
     8	## The forcing question
     9	
    10	rpg-api#793 wires the composition into the game as a coexisting
    11	encounter type. The wire speaks one dungeon-absolute space — a
    12	deliberate choice: *"we left that per room because it put load on the
    13	web to connect and build dungeons from separate rooms."* And movement
    14	crosses rooms: *"pathing goes from room to room."* The composition's
    15	`Move` is same-room by documented v1 constraint, and wave 1's
    16	`ConnectionInput{ID, From, To}` is declared but inert. Multi-room free
    17	roam blocks on giving that topology teeth.
    18	
    19	## Decisions
    20	
    21	### 1. The composition owns the topology (confirmed, not new)
    22	
    23	Wave 1 already put connections in `FieldInput`; v0.2 makes them do
    24	something. The alternative — an adapter-only `Transfer` verb where
    25	rpg-api decides what's traversable — was rejected because deciders live
    26	at the composition level: if the composition doesn't know rooms
    27	connect, **a monster can never chase a player through a doorway**.
    28	Pursuit would die at every room boundary, capping monster behavior at
    29	single-room forever and quietly moving rules truth (what is
    30	traversable) out of the rulebook.
    31	
    32	### 2. Openings only — no door state
    33	
    34	Kirk: *"our freeroam can open doors and it can actually be simplified
    35	if that helps us. we can get there when we get there."* The live game's
    36	door interaction is explicitly not a parity requirement. Connections in
    37	v0.2 are always-open openings. Door state (open/closed/locked,
    38	Interact semantics, probably interrupt windows) is a later wave.
    39	
    40	### 3. Sight stays room-scoped
    41	
    42	Connections do not transmit line of sight in this version. Crossing a
    43	boundary is how you learn what's there — good dungeon-crawl texture,
    44	and it keeps v0.2 from inheriting surprise cross-room occlusion math.
    45	Cross-room LoS becomes its own considered feature later, not a freebie.
    46	
    47	### 4. Traversal is an explicit verb, not Move magic
    48	
    49	`Move` stays same-room and honest. A new `Traverse` verb crosses a
    50	connection: the member must be standing at one endpoint; they arrive at
    51	the other. The server already owns pathing in the absolute space, so a
    52	cross-room path decomposes at the adapter into move → traverse → move.
    53	Implicit auto-transition on `Move` was rejected as unfalsifiable magic:
    54	the explicit verb gives a pinnable beat and a crisp precondition.
    55	
    56	### 5. Deciders learn where they stand (resolving the wave-1 gap)
    57	
    58	`Decide(view []intel.Holding)` has no self-placement — flagged at
    59	wave-1 ratification as the View own-placement gap. It bites for real
    60	now: a decider cannot pick a doorway without knowing which room it is
    61	in. v0.2 resolves the gap in the direction the wave-1 design originally
    62	promised: the decider receives a snapshot of its own room + position
    63	alongside its holdings. Static field topology is not secret — deciders
    64	may be constructed knowing the map; what they must never receive is
    65	other members' live truth (C2 stands).
    66	
    67	### 6. Intent vocabulary grows `IntentTraverse`
    68	
    69	Pursuit through an opening is a decision like any other: decided in
    70	phase 1, executed in phase 2, atomic under R5. A goblin that saw you
    71	slip into the hall holds a ghost whose payload names the room — it can
    72	choose the connection that leads there.
    73	
    74	### 7. No dungeon-builder coupling
    75	
    76	Kirk: dungeon builder *"spec 0.4 is not verified and 0.3 is not really
    77	playable."* The composition's authoring surface stays `SetupInput`;
    78	rpg-api's wave-1 dungeon keys use a minimal direct spec. Nothing here
    79	consumes or emits the dungeon-builder pipeline.
    80	
    81	### 8. Rooms choose their grid (added 2026-08-11, Platform pushback)
    82	
    83	Platform flagged the composition's square-grid usage against the
    84	hex-cube wire. The truth: spatial underneath is the same hex engine
    85	the old module ships to the wire (`GridShape`, `NewHexGrid`, cube
    86	coordinates, all LoS/adjacency behind the Grid interface); the
    87	composition merely *chose* square at its two grid-construction sites.
    88	v0.2 makes the choice per-room: `RoomInput` gains a `GridShape`
    89	(zero value = square, fully compatible), and in-bounds validation
    90	defers to the grid's own validity check instead of rectangle math.
    91	Rooms constructed hex make the wire projection identity rather than a
    92	lossy square→hex remap.
    93	
    94	### 9. Version and compatibility
    95	
    96	`v0.2.0`, additive in spirit. Two honest compat notes, both acceptable
    97	at zero external consumers (rpg-api is not wired yet): connection
    98	validation tightens (endpoints become required), and the `Decider`
    99	interface signature changes. Both are called out in the design.
   100	
   101	## Shelved (future us answers better than today us)
   102	
   103	- Door state, locks, and their Interact/interrupt semantics.
   104	- Cross-room line of sight through openings.
   105	- One-way or conditional connections (chutes, portcullises).
   106	- Combat chaining at a doorway (rides #916).
